topic: 7 strange real borders, ending with India's enclave swap, with the Korean DMZ wildlife haven at number two
hook: Your home address could once have been India, inside Bangladesh, inside India, inside Bangladesh.
title: 7 Real Borders Stranger Than Fiction
description:
Seven real borders that make no sense, from an American town you can only reach through Canada to a Korean war zone that became a wildlife haven. The last one is in India, where a single field once sat four layers deep inside two countries. Watch to the end to see how it was finally fixed.

#borders #geography #india

scenes.narration: Your home address could once have been India, inside Bangladesh, inside India, inside Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Four Layers Deep

scenes.narration: That place is number one on today's list of seven borders that make no sense.
scenes.headline: Number One Is Real

scenes.narration: Before it, you will see an American town you can only reach through Canada, and a runway that stops traffic.
scenes.headline: A Runway For Traffic

scenes.narration: You will also see a war zone that became a wildlife haven. The last border is in India.
scenes.headline: War Zone, Wildlife

scenes.narration: Quick promise: by the end, you will see why India wins this list by a mile.
scenes.headline: India Wins

scenes.narration: Every one of these is real, and each is stranger than the one before. Let's start.
scenes.headline: Let's Count Down

scenes.narration: Number seven. Your drive home can cross two international borders, and you never leave your own country.
scenes.headline: Number Seven

scenes.narration: Point Roberts is a small piece of Washington state in the USA, hanging off the bottom of Canada's British Columbia.
scenes.headline: American Town

scenes.narration: The border follows the 49th parallel, and this tip of land fell just south of it. So it belongs to America.
scenes.headline: The 49th Parallel

scenes.narration: But no road inside America reaches it. To get there by land, you must drive into Canada, then back out again.
scenes.headline: Through Canada

scenes.narration: That means a passport check going in, and another one coming out, just to reach a town that is American.
scenes.headline: Two Checks

scenes.narration: The reason is a straight line drawn on a map long ago, with no thought for the land underneath it.
scenes.headline: A Pen Line

scenes.narration: For the people who live there, it is just how the road works.
scenes.headline: Normal Life

scenes.narration: A pen stroke left an American town stuck on a Canadian peninsula. Easy so far. Number six is weirder.
scenes.headline: It Gets Weirder

scenes.narration: Number six. There is a Spanish town sitting fully inside France, and it has been that way for centuries.
scenes.headline: Number Six

scenes.narration: It is called Llivia, in the Pyrenees mountains, and French land surrounds it on every side.
scenes.headline: Spain Inside France

scenes.narration: In 1659 a treaty gave France a set of villages. But Llivia was officially a town, not a village, so it stayed Spanish.
scenes.headline: Town Not Village

scenes.narration: One legal word, and a town stayed trapped inside another country. That tiny technical detail is the whole reason.
scenes.headline: One Legal Word

scenes.narration: A short road links it to Spain, and that road is treated as a special corridor.
scenes.headline: The Special Road

scenes.narration: You can walk its streets, and a museum in the town tells the story of its strange position.
scenes.headline: A Museum Of It

scenes.narration: Spanish streets, Spanish shops, and French fields on every side. Now let's go where a border meets an airport runway.
scenes.headline: Next: A Runway

scenes.narration: Number five. Imagine walking out of a country on foot, and a plane landing right in front of you.
scenes.headline: Number Five

scenes.narration: That is Gibraltar, a British territory on Spain's southern tip. The road into town crosses the airport runway itself.
scenes.headline: Road Crosses Runway

scenes.narration: When a plane lands or takes off, barriers come down, and cars, bikes and people simply wait. A red light for airplanes.
scenes.headline: Red Light For Planes

scenes.narration: Then the barrier goes up, and everyone walks across the same strip of tarmac where a jet touched down minutes ago.
scenes.headline: Walk The Tarmac

scenes.narration: Spain disputes who owns the land under that runway, so the whole crossing sits on an argument over the border.
scenes.headline: Who Owns It?

scenes.narration: You also pass border officers on the way in and out, so you cross a country line and an airfield together.
scenes.headline: Border Plus Airfield

scenes.narration: A border, a runway and a traffic light in one spot. Next, a region cut off from its own country.
scenes.headline: Cut Off Next

scenes.narration: Number four. There is a part of Russia that you cannot reach from Russia without leaving Russia.
scenes.headline: Number Four

scenes.narration: It is called Kaliningrad, on the Baltic Sea, squeezed between Poland and Lithuania. The rest of Russia is far away.
scenes.headline: Russia, Detached

scenes.narration: Before 1945 it was the German city of Königsberg. After the Second World War, the Soviet Union took it over.
scenes.headline: Once Königsberg

scenes.narration: Then the Soviet Union broke up, and Lithuania and others became independent countries. That left Kaliningrad cut off from the mainland.
scenes.headline: Then It Split

scenes.narration: Now trains from mainland Russia must pass through Lithuania, and travellers need special transit documents.
scenes.headline: Special Transit Papers

scenes.narration: Imagine a state of India you could only visit by passing through another country. That is Kaliningrad's situation for Russia.
scenes.headline: Like Cut-Off India

scenes.narration: And this is not a village. It is a whole region with a major seaport on the Baltic coast.
scenes.headline: A Whole Region

scenes.narration: Cut off by land and joined only by paperwork. Number three uses two currencies on the same street.
scenes.headline: Two Currencies

scenes.narration: Number three. There is a German town where shops take Swiss francs, and cars carry a special number plate.
scenes.headline: Number Three

scenes.narration: It is called Büsingen, and Switzerland surrounds it completely. You cannot reach it from Germany without crossing Swiss land.
scenes.headline: Germany Inside Swiss

scenes.narration: It is German, but it sits inside the Swiss customs area, so Swiss francs and euros are both part of daily life.
scenes.headline: Francs And Euros

scenes.narration: Think of paying for chai in euros in one shop, and in francs in the next.
scenes.headline: Chai In Francs

scenes.narration: Its cars even carry their own letters, BÜS, so a number plate alone tells you it is this one odd little town.
scenes.headline: Plate: BÜS

scenes.narration: Residents can vote in German elections, yet their daily life is wired to Switzerland.
scenes.headline: German Vote, Swiss Life

scenes.narration: German citizens in a place that works a lot like Switzerland. A border that is real, but easy to forget.
scenes.headline: Easy To Forget

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places like these, subscribe, because the last two are the ones people send to their friends.
scenes.headline: Subscribe For More

scenes.narration: And number two is not a village or a town. It is a strip of land where a war is still on paper.
scenes.headline: A War On Paper

scenes.narration: Number two. A war zone that turned into one of the best wildlife havens you can see on a satellite map.
scenes.headline: Number Two

scenes.narration: It is the Korean DMZ, the demilitarised zone between North Korea and South Korea. It is about four kilometres wide.
scenes.headline: 4 km Wide

scenes.narration: It was drawn in 1953, when the Korean War ended with a ceasefire. A full peace treaty never followed.
scenes.headline: Ceasefire, Not Peace

scenes.narration: Both sides keep soldiers close, and parts of the ground are mined. So for decades almost nobody has lived or farmed here.
scenes.headline: Nobody Lives Here

scenes.narration: And that is the twist. With people gone, nature moved in. The most guarded strip of land became a quiet green corridor.
scenes.headline: Nature Moved In

scenes.narration: Rare birds live there, including cranes, the tall white birds that Koreans see as a symbol of long life.
scenes.headline: Cranes In A War Zone

scenes.narration: Look at it on a satellite image and you can see a green belt cutting across the peninsula between two countries at odds.
scenes.headline: A Green Belt

scenes.narration: Barbed wire and watchtowers on both sides, and in the middle, birds that do not know there is a border.
scenes.headline: Birds Ignore Borders

scenes.narration: Many conservationists now call it an accidental nature reserve, and hope it is protected for good.
scenes.headline: Accidental Reserve

scenes.narration: One of the most tense borders on Earth is also a nature reserve by accident. Now, number one, in India.
scenes.headline: Now: India

scenes.narration: Number one. This is the border from the start of the video, and it is the strangest border story on the list.
scenes.headline: Number One

scenes.narration: Along the India and Bangladesh border, there were small islands of land belonging to the other country.
scenes.headline: Islands Of Land

scenes.narration: The area is Cooch Behar, in the north of West Bengal, not far from Assam and Bhutan.
scenes.headline: Cooch Behar

scenes.narration: Indian villages stood inside Bangladesh, and Bangladeshi villages stood inside India. These pockets are called enclaves.
scenes.headline: Enclaves

scenes.narration: Residents were cut off from their own country, and many struggled to get basic services like roads, schools and electricity.
scenes.headline: Cut Off

scenes.narration: One patch, Dahala Khagrabari, was Indian land inside Bangladeshi land, inside Indian land, inside Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Dahala Khagrabari

scenes.narration: Four layers of borders in one small field. It was known as the world's only enclave of that kind.
scenes.headline: Four Layers

scenes.narration: People lived in these pockets for decades, holding the citizenship of a country they could barely reach.
scenes.headline: Decades In Limbo

scenes.narration: Finally, on the night of 31 July 2015, India and Bangladesh began swapping the enclaves. By midnight, 1 August, it was official.
scenes.headline: Midnight Swap

scenes.narration: India handed over 111 enclaves to Bangladesh, and received 51 in return. Residents could choose which country to live in.
scenes.headline: 111 And 51

scenes.narration: After decades in limbo, thousands of people finally got a country with an address, roads and a government.
scenes.headline: A Real Address

scenes.narration: So the address from the start of this video was real. A map once had India inside Bangladesh inside India inside Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: The Address Was Real

scenes.narration: These leftovers came from old land deals between local rulers, which were never tidied up when later borders were drawn.
scenes.headline: Old Royal Deals

scenes.narration: It took until 2015 to fix them, and it is remembered as a rare, peaceful border swap.
scenes.headline: A Peaceful Swap

scenes.narration: So yes, your address really could have been India inside Bangladesh inside India inside Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Back To The Start

scenes.narration: Next video: more places where the map and the ground disagree.
scenes.headline: Next Video
